papers.title: Thermostable Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes for High-Temperature Biomass Conversion: From Molecular Design to Process Integration.
papers.abstract: High-temperature processing of carbohydrate-rich biomass, including starch liquefaction and lignocellulose saccharification, can improve sugar yields, reduce contamination risks, and facilitate integration with thermochemical pretreatments. However, the operational stability of native carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) at 60-90 °C remains a major bottleneck for efficient and economically viable biorefineries, and existing reviews rarely integrate multiscale molecular mechanisms with process-relevant engineering strategies. This review systematically examines the multiscale basis of thermost
papers.summary: This review examines the molecular and structural basis of thermostability in carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) used for high-temperature biomass processing, such as starch liquefaction and lignocellulose saccharification at 60-90 °C. It connects mechanistic insights from protein engineering and molecular design to process-level integration strategies for biorefineries. The work aims to bridge the gap between fundamental thermostability research and practical industrial enzyme deployment.

papers.title: Syndirella: synthesis-directed fragment elaboration enables extensive and cost-effective binding site exploration beyond catalog compounds.
papers.abstract: Fragment screens provide an information-rich starting point for designing derivative compounds in structure-based drug discovery. However, derivatives in the fragment-to-hit stage are typically designed from only one or a few fragments, risking premature convergence on an unproductive series and dramatically limiting exploration of the binding site's interaction opportunities. This is avoidable by exploring a broad, chemically diverse set of scaffolds and elaborations spanning interactions revealed across many fragments, as well as those not yet observed. Conventional catalog procurement makes
papers.summary: Syndirella is a computational tool that designs derivative compounds from fragment screening hits by systematically elaborating multiple fragment scaffolds rather than focusing on just one or a few. This synthesis-directed approach enables broader, more cost-effective exploration of binding site interactions beyond what is available in commercial catalogs, reducing the risk of premature convergence on unproductive chemical series in fragment-to-hit drug discovery.

papers.title: Structure-Based Engineering for PTPσ-Targeted Therapeutic Development.
papers.abstract: Protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPσ) is a member of the leukocyte common antigen-related (LAR) family of receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases. Its architecture integrates an extracellular proteoglycan-sensing region, a single-pass transmembrane helix, and tandem intracellular phosphatase domains. In neural injury, inhibition of PTPσ signaling can relieve chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan (CSPG)-mediated restriction of axonal growth and plasticity. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA), by contrast, restoration of PTPσ activity in fibroblast-like synoviocytes can suppress pathogenic migration
papers.summary: This review discusses structure-based protein engineering strategies targeting PTPσ, a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase involved in neural injury and rheumatoid arthritis. The authors describe how PTPσ's architecture—extracellular proteoglycan-sensing region, transmembrane helix, and tandem intracellular phosphatase domains—can be exploited for therapeutic design. The key insight is context-dependent: inhibiting PTPσ promotes axonal growth after neural injury, while restoring its activity in rheumatoid arthritis suppresses pathogenic synoviocyte migration.

papers.title: Plasma Carrier Proteins as Supramolecular Nanovectors for Cancer Therapy: The Trojan Horse Approach.
papers.abstract: Conventional chemotherapeutics often suffer from poor aqueous solubility, short circulation half-lives, lack of tumor selectivity, and present dose-limiting systemic toxicity. This perspective examines the Trojan Horse Approach (THA), in which plasma carrier proteins (PCPs) are exploited as discrete, non-covalent supramolecular hosts for chemotherapeutic agents, and discusses its potential to overcome the limitations of both free drugs and conventional protein nanoparticles. Two principal strategies for assembling ex vivo drug-protein complexes are discussed: (i) molecular recognition, in whic
papers.summary: This perspective article discusses the Trojan Horse Approach, which uses plasma carrier proteins (like albumin) as natural nanocarriers that bind chemotherapy drugs non-covalently and deliver them to tumors. The authors argue this strategy could overcome problems of conventional chemo such as poor solubility, short half-life, and systemic toxicity, and they compare assembly strategies based on molecular recognition versus other methods.

papers.title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation.
papers.abstract: Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
papers.summary: This study identifies a single dominant 'water-pinning' hot spot that allows intrinsically disordered tau to stack in register and form seed-competent fibrils capable of templated aggregation. The pinning mechanism is proposed to prevent mismatched stacking of tau molecules onto fibril seeds, explaining how disordered tau achieves ordered, prion-like propagation. Structured solvation appears central to this templating process.

papers.title: In silico approach to Helicobacter pylori vaccine design.
papers.abstract: Helicobacter pylori, a Gram-negative microorganism, infects over half of the human population worldwide. Its extensive genetic variability and capacity to bypass host immune defences continue to impede the creation of an effective vaccine. Nonetheless, contemporary progress in computational biology and immunoinformatics has introduced innovative methodologies that can substantially support and accelerate vaccine design against this pathogen. In the present work, an in silico strategy was employed to develop a multi-epitope vaccine targeting H. pylori. The FlaA, UreB and PSA D15 proteins were c
papers.summary: This paper describes an in silico multi-epitope vaccine design against Helicobacter pylori, combining epitopes from the FlaA, UreB, and PSA D15 proteins. The approach uses computational biology and immunoinformatics to address the pathogen's genetic variability and immune evasion, which have hindered traditional vaccine development. The work is a computational design study without experimental validation.

papers.title: The lysis mechanism of the haloarchaeal virus HFTV1.
papers.abstract: Tailed bacteriophages can lyse their host with help of the holin-endolysin system. However, for archaeal tailed viruses (arTVs), whose archaeal hosts have a fundamentally different cell envelope, lysis mechanisms are unknown. In this study, we use the model archaeal virus-host system: Haloferax tailed virus 1 (HFTV1), which infects the methanobacteriote Haloferax gibbonsii LR2-5. We identified and characterized the lysis protein GP33, a small membrane protein that has no sequence homology with bacterial holins. Overexpression resulted in cell lysis, and the protein forms foci near the cell env
papers.summary: This study identifies and characterizes GP33, a small membrane protein that mediates lysis of the archaeal host Haloferax gibbonsii by the tailed archaeal virus HFTV1. GP33 has no sequence homology to bacterial holins but forms foci near the cell envelope and causes lysis when overexpressed, revealing a distinct archaeal lysis mechanism. The work provides the first mechanistic insight into how archaeal tailed viruses lyse their hosts, whose cell envelopes differ fundamentally from bacteria.

papers.title: Substrate-bound structures of yeast ALA synthase reveal protein dynamics initiating heme biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: Heme is an essential prosthetic group involved in multiple biological processes in nearly all organisms. Heme biosynthesis is initiated by the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzyme aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS). Mutations in ALAS cause multiple hematological diseases. Despite sharing approximately 70% sequence similarity, ALAS homologs exhibit distinct expression and regulatory mechanisms. However, the molecular basis for their functional divergence remains poorly understood. Here, we used x-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations to elucidate the structure and dynamics
papers.summary: This study presents substrate-bound crystal structures of yeast aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS), the enzyme that initiates heme biosynthesis, combined with molecular dynamics simulations. The structures reveal protein dynamics that accompany substrate binding and help explain how ALAS homologs with ~70% sequence similarity diverge functionally and regulatorily. These insights provide a structural basis for understanding disease-causing ALAS mutations.

papers.title: Harnessing the ubiquitin-proteasome system: advances and challenges of PROTACs in breast cancer.
papers.abstract: Breast cancer is one of the most significant health issues in the world, and resistance to treatment and a lack of targets that can be addressed with drugs limit the effectiveness of the existing treatment options. The development of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) has shifted the concept of occupancy-based inhibition toward event-based targeted protein degradation. Avoiding ubiquitin-proteasome hijacking, PROTACs target disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases, allowing them to be catalytically degraded, thereby eliminating formerly undruggable or resistant targets. Their modular desi
papers.summary: This review discusses proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), a class of molecules that recruit disease-relevant proteins to E3 ligases for degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system, as a strategy for breast cancer therapy. It highlights how PROTACs can address previously undruggable or treatment-resistant targets and surveys advances and remaining challenges in their development.

papers.title: Different dynamic behaviors between asymmetric catenanes and bonded rings.
papers.abstract: A hybrid mesoscopic simulation scheme integrating multi-particle collision dynamics (MPCD) and molecular dynamics (MD) was adopted to probe the dynamic responses and conformational evolution of semi-flexible asymmetric mechanically linked ([2]catenanes, PC) and chemically bonded (bonded rings, BR) ring polymers with different linkage modes under shear flow fields. First, by analyzing the prolateness, asphericity, and three-dimensional surface area of the ring, we reveal that the rings of asymmetric PC and BR adopt an identical conformation as a disc-like structure, whereas the symmetric PC and
papers.summary: This study uses hybrid mesoscopic simulations (MPCD + MD) to compare how asymmetric mechanically linked catenanes and chemically bonded ring polymers respond to shear flow. Both asymmetric architectures adopt similar disc-like conformations, but their dynamic responses and conformational evolution differ due to the linkage mode. The work clarifies how mechanical vs. chemical linkage affects ring polymer dynamics under flow.

papers.title: Phospholipase Fluorogenic Probes and Molecular Determinants of Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate-Adenosine Monophosphate Binding to Cyclic Oligonucleotide-Based Antiphage Signaling System CapV.
papers.abstract: Cyclic oligonucleotide-based antiphage signaling systems (CBASS) protect bacteria from bacteriophage infection by producing cyclic nucleotide second messengers that activate downstream effector proteins. Cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate (cGAMP)-activated phospholipase in Vibrio (CapV) is a prevalent CBASS effector whose activity is commonly monitored using the commercially available fluorogenic substrate resorufin butyrate; however, this probe is hydrolyzed by both basal and activated CapV, limiting its usefulness in CapV-related studies. Here, we report the rational desi
papers.summary: The authors developed improved fluorogenic probes for measuring CapV phospholipase activity, addressing the limitation that the standard resorufin butyrate substrate is hydrolyzed by both basal and activated enzyme. They also identified molecular determinants governing how cGAMP binds to and activates CapV within bacterial CBASS antiphage defense systems. This work provides better tools for studying CBASS effector activation and clarifies the structural basis of cyclic nucleotide recognition.

papers.title: Zinc peroxide-coated gold nanorods as the therapeutic adjuvants for photothermal enhanced chemodynamic therapy and metalloimmunotherapy against tumor.
papers.abstract: Traditional tumor therapies have limited efficacy, leading to a high mortality rate. Although immunotherapy holds considerable therapeutic promise, clinical immunotherapy for solid tumors only elicits durable responses in a minority of patients. This limitation is largely attributed to the highly immunosuppressive nature of the tumor microenvironment (TME). Notably, conventional chemodynamic therapy (CDT) is hampered by endogenous hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) shortage in tumor cells, and AZP compensates this defect via in-situ H2O2 self-supplementation to amplify hydroxyl radical generation.
papers.summary: This study develops gold nanorods coated with zinc peroxide (AZP) as a multifunctional therapeutic adjuvant for cancer treatment. The zinc peroxide coating self-supplies hydrogen peroxide within tumor cells, overcoming the typical shortage that limits chemodynamic therapy, while the gold nanorods enable photothermal therapy. Together, these effects amplify hydroxyl radical generation and stimulate metalloimmunotherapy, potentially reversing the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment to improve treatment responses.

papers.title: Diversification and functional expansion of archaeal T4F machineries.
papers.abstract: Archaea have several cell surface structures belonging to the type 4 filament (T4F) superfamily. All share a minimal core assembly system consisting of an ATPase, a platform protein, a filament-forming protein, and a class III signal peptidase. Here, we generated novel MacSyFinder2 models to identify and classify archaeal T4F systems. Our analysis revealed a vast diversity of archaeal T4F, with many organisms harboring one or more assembly machineries. Structure-based phylogenetic analysis showed that the variable N-terminal domain of T4F-related ATPases mirrors the subsystem clustering, indic
papers.summary: This study developed new MacSyFinder2 models to systematically identify and classify type 4 filament (T4F) systems across archaea, revealing a much greater diversity of these cell surface structures than previously recognized, with many organisms carrying multiple distinct machineries. Structure-based phylogenetic analysis showed that the variable N-terminal domain of T4F-related ATPases tracks with subsystem clustering, suggesting functional diversification tied to structural variation. The work expands the known repertoire of archaeal surface structures and provides a classification framework for future study.

papers.title: On the binding of cell-adhesive proteins vitronectin, fibronectin and laminin to agarose hydrogel.
papers.abstract: Protein binding at hydrogel interfaces is a key process in biomaterials surface science, governing the biochemical response of cells. Here, we investigate the binding behavior of three cell-adhesive proteins with distinct molecular weights, namely, vitronectin, fibronectin, and laminin on a hydrogel network composed of a low-hydrophobic agarose. Binding kinetics was evaluated through a solution-depletion method. Using destabilizing agents such as the chaotropic salt magnesium perchlorate, Mg(ClO4)2, or the non-ionic surfactant Tween 20, our results show that binding is driven by hydrophobic ef
papers.summary: This study examines how three cell-adhesive proteins (vitronectin, fibronectin, and laminin) bind to agarose hydrogels, using solution-depletion kinetics and destabilizing agents to probe the mechanism. The results indicate that binding is driven primarily by hydrophobic interactions, with the chaotropic salt Mg(ClO4)2 and the surfactant Tween 20 disrupting protein adsorption. The work clarifies the interfacial biochemistry governing cell responses to hydrogel biomaterials.

papers.title: Accelerating the discovery of nanoporous gas separation materials via Coulomb-enhanced classical density functional theory.
papers.abstract: The design of advanced nanoporous materials for gas separations, such as carbon capture and alkyne purification, is increasingly driven by high-throughput screening. However, the accurate description of electrostatic interactions in porous frameworks remains challenging and can introduce sizable deviations between predicted and experimental performance, thereby hindering rational materials design. To address this gap, we present a computational framework, compatible with standard force fields under appropriate charge assignments, that explicitly incorporates a point-charge model to capture ads
papers.summary: The paper presents a computational framework that enhances classical density functional theory with an explicit point-charge model to better capture electrostatic interactions in nanoporous materials. This improves the accuracy of predicting gas adsorption and separation performance, facilitating high-throughput screening for applications like carbon capture and alkyne purification. The method is compatible with standard force fields, making it broadly applicable for rational materials design.

papers.title: Integrated Experimental and Computational Investigation of Fluorinated Benzoylthiourea Derivatives: Structural Characterization, Hirshfeld Surface Analysis, Antioxidant Activity, and MAO-B Inhibitory Potential for Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Three novel fluorinated benzoylthiourea derivatives, namely FBTU1-FBTU3, were successfully synthesized in 79-86% yields and fully characterized using spectroscopic techniques including FT-IR, 1H, 13C and 19F NMR, UV-Vis spectroscopy, elemental analysis, and single-crystal X-ray diffraction (SCXRD). All three compounds crystallize in the monoclinic system (P21/c for FBTU1 and FBTU3; P21/n for FBTU2) with Z = 4. The crystallographic analysis revealed well-defined molecular geometries stabilized by intramolecular and intermolecular interactions. Hirshfeld surface and energy framework analyses ind
papers.summary: The authors synthesized three new fluorinated benzoylthiourea compounds and characterized them using spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography, revealing their crystal packing and intermolecular interactions via Hirshfeld surface analysis. They also evaluated these compounds for antioxidant activity and MAO-B inhibition, a target relevant to Parkinson's disease. The study integrates experimental structural work with computational analysis to assess the compounds' potential bioactivity.

papers.title: Integration of Network Toxicology and Machine Learning to Prioritize Candidate Molecular Features Associated with NNK-Related Lung Cancer.
papers.abstract: 4-(Methylnitrosamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone (NNK) is a tobacco-specific nitrosamine implicated in tobacco-related lung carcinogenesis. Its biological effects in vivo depend substantially on metabolic conversion to NNAL and cytochrome P450-mediated formation of reactive intermediates. In this study, predicted NNK-associated proteins were integrated with lung cancer transcriptomic data sets, followed by network analysis and machine-learning-based feature prioritization. Five genes, SNAI2, PLAU, DNMT3A, FAP, and CCNB1, were prioritized based on their contributions to the multigene classificati
papers.summary: This study combined network toxicology predictions of NNK-interacting proteins with lung cancer transcriptomic datasets and machine learning to prioritize candidate molecular features. Five genes (SNAI2, PLAU, DNMT3A, FAP, and CCNB1) were identified as top contributors to a multigene classification model for NNK-related lung cancer. The work offers a computational framework for linking a tobacco carcinogen to candidate biomarkers, though experimental validation is not reported.

papers.title: Benchmarking Affinity-Based Docking for Irreversible Acetylcholinesterase Inhibitors: A Physics-Informed Reactivity Framework for Stereoselective Potency Prioritization.
papers.abstract: Irreversible organophosphorus inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) act by covalent phosphylation of the catalytic serine, yet their computational prioritization is often based on affinity scores from noncovalent docking. We benchmark that assumption against a curated set of measured human-AChE inhibition rate constants (n = 14; G-, V-, and organophosphate-pesticide classes, including a configuration-resolved VX pair). AutoDock Vina affinity (Spearman ρ = +0.12) and GNINA CNN scores (ρ = -0.40) do not provide statistically reliable potency rankings; explicit covalent docking also remains w
papers.summary: This study tests whether standard noncovalent docking scores can rank the potency of irreversible organophosphorus acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which act by covalently modifying the catalytic serine. Benchmarking against measured inhibition rate constants for 14 compounds, the authors find that AutoDock Vina affinity and GNINA CNN scores fail to reliably rank potency, and even explicit covalent docking remains limited. They propose a physics-informed reactivity framework to better prioritize stereoselective potency.

papers.title: Integrated In Silico Analysis Reveals ABC Transporter ATP-Binding Protein as a Therapeutic Target in Helicobacter pylori.
papers.abstract: Helicobacter pylori remains a major cause of gastric diseases, while increasing antimicrobial resistance highlights the need for novel therapeutic targets. Here, we developed a comprehensive computational target-prioritization framework integrating Rosetta Stone domain-fusion analysis, subtractive genomics, metabolic pathway mapping, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations to identify pathogen-specific drug targets in H. pylori J99. Twelve conserved domain families comprising 746 proteins were identified, and domain abundance showed a weak negative correlation with versatility
papers.summary: This study uses a computational pipeline combining domain-fusion analysis, subtractive genomics, metabolic pathway mapping, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics to prioritize drug targets in Helicobacter pylori J99. The authors identify an ABC transporter ATP-binding protein as a promising pathogen-specific therapeutic target, addressing the need for new targets given rising antimicrobial resistance. The work is entirely in silico and would require experimental validation.

papers.title: Exploring the Molecular Mechanism of Ganoderic Acid B for Insomnia Based on Metabolomics, Network Pharmacology, Molecular Docking, and Experimental Validation.
papers.abstract: Objective: Ganoderma lucidum, a fungus of the genus Ganoderma in the family Polyporaceae, is often used in traditional medicine for the treatment of insomnia and amnesia, etc. Ganoderic acid B, a characteristic lanostane-type triterpenoid isolated from Ganoderma lucidum, has been preliminarily verified to possess mild sedative activity in existing studies. This study aims to explore the potential regulatory mechanism of Ganoderic acid B against PCPA-induced insomnia-like damage via multiple preclinical research strategies, and provide preliminary molecular and experimental clues for subsequent
papers.summary: This study investigates how ganoderic acid B, a compound from the medicinal fungus Ganoderma lucidum, may alleviate insomnia. Using metabolomics, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and experimental validation in a PCPA-induced insomnia model, the authors identify potential molecular targets and pathways underlying its sedative effects. The work provides preliminary mechanistic clues for a traditional medicine-derived compound.

papers.title: An Active Learning Framework for PFAS-Free Surfactant Discovery in Firefighting Foams.
papers.abstract: The growing concerns over the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in firefighting foams have necessitated the development of efficient discovery frameworks for eco-friendly alternatives. In this work, we demonstrate an integrated pipeline leveraging active learning and coarse-grained (CG) molecular dynamics simulations to explore the design space of single-tail hydrocarbon surfactants for inhibiting fuel transport across interfaces. We design a targeted chemical space of 12,124 CG surfactants, represented by latent vectors learned from molecular graph
papers.summary: This paper presents an active learning pipeline that combines coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning to search a large chemical space of 12,124 single-tail hydrocarbon surfactants as PFAS-free alternatives for firefighting foams. The framework uses latent vector representations learned from molecular graphs to guide the discovery of surfactants that inhibit fuel transport across interfaces. It demonstrates how active learning can efficiently navigate a targeted chemical design space for environmentally friendly foam formulations.

papers.title: Molecular Characterization of Lasmiditan Binding to Human Serum Albumin: Site Preference, Structural Response, and Binding Energetics.
papers.abstract: Human serum albumin (HSA), the major transport protein in blood plasma, can substantially influence the distribution of therapeutic compounds. Although lasmiditan (LASMI) is a recently introduced antimigraine drug with reported moderate plasma protein binding, the molecular determinants of its association with HSA remain poorly defined. Here, an integrated spectroscopic and computational approach was used to characterize HSA-LASMI complex formation, binding-site preference, and the accompanying structural response of the protein. UV-Vis absorption, steady-state fluorescence quenching, FTIR, an
papers.summary: This study uses spectroscopy and computational modeling to characterize how the antimigraine drug lasmiditan binds to human serum albumin, the main transport protein in blood plasma. The authors identify the preferred binding site, describe how the protein's structure responds to drug binding, and quantify the energetics of the interaction. These molecular details help explain lasmiditan's moderate plasma protein binding and could inform understanding of its distribution in the body.

papers.title: Structural insights into the ligand modulation of MRGPRX4 conformational plasticity.
papers.abstract: Chronic pruritus is a debilitating condition with limited treatment options, particularly in cholestatic liver diseases, where bile acid dysregulation is a known trigger. Although Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X4 (MRGPRX4) has recently been identified as a key mediator of bile acid-induced pruritus, the structural mechanisms underlying its inhibition remain poorly understood, hindering the development of therapeutic antagonists. Here, we report the cryo-electron microscopy structures of MRGPRX4 in three distinct states: agonist-bound state, antagonist-bound state, and apo state. Our s
papers.summary: This study presents cryo-EM structures of the receptor MRGPRX4 in agonist-bound, antagonist-bound, and apo states, revealing how ligand binding reshapes the receptor's conformation. MRGPRX4 mediates bile acid-induced itching in cholestatic liver disease, so these structures provide a template for designing antagonist drugs to treat chronic pruritus.

papers.title: Design of ancestral protein-glutaminase with improved thermal stability.
papers.abstract: Protein-glutaminase (PG) from Chryseobacterium proteolyticum is an industrially valuable enzyme for protein deamidation; however, its application is limited because of insufficient thermal stability. Previous rational design studies have enhanced the thermostability of PG but often required labor-intensive, stepwise optimization. In this study, ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) was used to engineer thermostable PG variants in a single design step. Eight ancestral PGs were constructed, all of which exhibited enhanced thermal stability compared with that of the wild type. The most stable v
papers.summary: The authors used ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) to engineer protein-glutaminase variants with improved thermal stability in a single design step, rather than through labor-intensive stepwise rational design. Eight reconstructed ancestral enzymes all showed enhanced thermostability relative to the wild type, with the most stable variant outperforming it. This demonstrates ASR as an efficient strategy for improving industrially relevant enzyme properties.

papers.title: Integrative pan-cancer analysis of AKT1 and structure-based drug design by buckwheat derived compounds.
papers.abstract: Copyright: © 2026 Sheikh et al. This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY 4.0), which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original author and source are credited. AKT1 is a serine-threonine protein-kinase involved in tumour cell proliferation, survival, metabolism, and therapeutic resistance via activation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway. However, the comprehensive pan-cancer characterization of AKT1 and systematics identifications of natural AKT1 inhibitors remains limited. T
papers.summary: This study performs a pan-cancer analysis of AKT1, a kinase in the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, to characterize its expression and role across tumor types, and then uses structure-based drug design to screen buckwheat-derived natural compounds as potential AKT1 inhibitors. The work combines multi-omics tumor data with molecular docking to nominate natural-product candidates targeting AKT1.

papers.title: Large-scale prospective evaluation of co-folding across hundreds of Mac1-ligand complexes and three virtual screens.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of ligand-bound protein complexes and ranking them by affinity are central problems in drug discovery. While deep-learning co-folding methods can help address these challenges, their evaluation has been hampered by the difficulties in assessing independence from training data and insufficiently large test sets. Here, we test the ability of co-folding methods to predict the structures of 551 ligands, 489 of which are of sufficient quality for evaluation, bound to the SARS-CoV-2 NSP3 macrodomain (Mac1) that were determined after the training cutoff dates. AlphaFold3 (AF3), Bo
papers.summary: This study prospectively tested deep-learning co-folding methods on 551 newly determined Mac1–ligand complexes, using structures solved after the models' training cutoffs to ensure a fair evaluation. AlphaFold3 and related methods were assessed for both structure prediction and affinity ranking across three virtual screens. The work provides a large, time-separated benchmark for judging how well co-folding generalizes to unseen ligand-bound complexes.

papers.title: PrOMet: Accurate and Robust Metal-Binding Site and Type Prediction.
papers.abstract: Metal binding to proteins is crucial for many biological functions, yet the prediction of metal-binding sites and metal types remains underexplored compared to other biomolecular interactions. Despite advances in deep learning, computational methods have achieved limited success in this area; even the best-reported approaches reach only moderate localization accuracy on high-resolution crystal structures, and even worse when applied to medium-resolution data. We hypothesize that the main challenge lies in the nature of metal binding. While the putative sites span the entire protein surface, ac
papers.summary: PrOMet is a new deep learning method for predicting where metals bind on protein surfaces and which metal type binds there. The authors argue that the difficulty lies in metal-binding sites being spread across the entire protein surface, and their approach improves localization accuracy over prior methods, including on medium-resolution structures.

papers.title: Protein interactions with small molecules, peptides and proteins share residue cluster classes.
papers.abstract: Macromolecular interactions with small molecules, peptides, and proteins are fundamental to cellular function. Despite intensive efforts to identify small-molecule modulators of protein-protein interactions (PPIs), successfully targeted interfaces remain rare, reinforcing the premise that binding sites across these molecular scale regimes possess distinct structural architectures. We previously demonstrated that the densest topological regions of protein structures, categorized as a collection of Residue Cluster Classes (cRCC), can effectively classify global protein folds and PPI. Here, we le
papers.summary: The authors extend their Residue Cluster Classes (cRCC) framework, which describes the densest topological regions of protein structures, to compare how proteins bind small molecules, peptides, and other proteins. They find that binding sites across these different molecular scales share common residue cluster class signatures, challenging the assumption that small-molecule and protein-protein interaction sites have fundamentally distinct architectures. This suggests cRCC-based analysis could help identify or design small-molecule modulators of protein-protein interfaces.

papers.title: Coupled effects of molecular weight and grafting density on protein adsorption in phosphorylcholine-based zwitterionic brushes.
papers.abstract: Zwitterionic polymer brushes are widely used to suppress nonspecific protein adsorption, yet their performance depends jointly on molecular weight and grafting density. Rational design remains difficult because these parameters are often examined separately or represented by a single conformational descriptor. Here, bovine serum albumin adsorption was systematically investigated across 22 poly(2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine) brush states prepared using a polydopamine-mediated grafting-to method that enabled systematic variation of molecular weight and grafting density. Quartz crystal
papers.journal: Journal of colloid and interface science
papers.summary: This study systematically varied both molecular weight and grafting density of zwitterionic phosphorylcholine polymer brushes across 22 states to understand how these coupled parameters control nonspecific protein adsorption. Using a polydopamine-mediated grafting method and quartz crystal microbalance measurements, the authors show that brush performance depends jointly on these two parameters rather than on either alone or a single conformational descriptor. The work provides a framework for rational design of antifouling surfaces.

papers.title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Quinoline CYP8B1 Inhibitors for the Potential Treatment of Metabolic Disease.
papers.abstract: CYP8B1 has been identified as a potential target for the treatment of metabolic diseases, such as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and type 2 diabetes (T2D). CYP8B1 enzyme inhibitor 1 was discovered from a high-throughput screen of our compound collection; however, its poor metabolic stability prevented further in vivo evaluation. Leveraging structure-based drug design, metabolite identification and metabolic stability-guided DMPK optimization, and library synthesis to rapidly expand SAR, we identified compound 9 with substantially improved DMPK properties. Compound 9 showed robust in
papers.summary: The authors optimized a quinoline-based CYP8B1 inhibitor series using structure-based drug design and DMPK-guided medicinal chemistry to overcome poor metabolic stability of an initial high-throughput screening hit. The resulting compound 9 shows substantially improved pharmacokinetic properties and is proposed as a candidate for treating metabolic diseases such as NAFLD and type 2 diabetes.

papers.title: Enhancing the Activity of Ribokinase from Thermus sp. 2.9 Through Rational Design for the Cascade Synthesis of Modified Nucleotides and Nucleosides.
papers.abstract: The pursuit of efficient approaches for the production of promising antiviral and cytostatic pharmaceuticals is a crucial direction in medical biotechnology, especially after the COVID-19 pandemic. Modified nucleosides and nucleotides represent a highly promising class of chemicals for the development of drugs against cancer and viral infections. Being an alternative to traditional chemical synthesis, cascades of nucleic exchange enzymes offer single-step synthesis of such compounds with exceptional stereo- and regioselectivity. Furthermore, employing thermostable enzymes for such cascades off
papers.summary: The authors used rational design to engineer a more active ribokinase from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus sp. 2.9, aiming to improve a multi-enzyme cascade for producing modified nucleosides and nucleotides. These compounds are valuable building blocks for antiviral and anticancer drugs, and thermostable enzymes enable more robust single-step synthesis with high stereo- and regioselectivity. The work demonstrates how protein engineering can enhance biocatalytic cascades for pharmaceutical production.

papers.title: Substituted diiminoisoindoles as anticancer agents: synthesis, structural characterization, and biological evaluation.
papers.abstract: Substituted diiminoisoindoles (DIIs), 1- 20, were synthesized as a nitrogen-rich scaffolds for evaluation of their anticancer activity. A streamlined one-pot lithiation/isoindole formation strategy enabled the preparation of a broad portfolio of dissymmetrically substituted DIIs from substituted anilines and dicarbonitrile precursors, with very good to excellent yields for most targets. Selected DIIs were further converted into DII-guanidine conjugates via carbodiimide-mediated guanylation. Structural characterization, including Z/E isomer distributions in solution and the solid-state, showed
papers.summary: The authors synthesized a library of 20 substituted diiminoisoindole (DII) compounds using a streamlined one-pot lithiation/isoindole formation strategy, and further derivatized some into DII-guanidine conjugates. They characterized the compounds structurally, including Z/E isomer distributions in solution and solid state, and evaluated them for anticancer activity. The work establishes DIIs as a nitrogen-rich scaffold for anticancer drug development.

papers.title: Benzothiazole-Derived Compounds as Potential Drugs for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes: A Descriptive Review.
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a multifactorial metabolic disease in which hyperglycemia coexists with insulin resistance, β-cell dysfunction, dyslipidemia, and progressive microvascular and macrovascular complications. The structural versatility of the benzothiazole scaffold has enabled the development of a diverse array of preclinical compounds capable of modulating multiple diabetes-relevant targets. This review critically analyzes the available evidence on benzothiazole-derived compounds exhibiting antidiabetic or other diabetes-related pharmacological activities. No lower publication-date limit
papers.summary: This review surveys benzothiazole-derived compounds that show preclinical antidiabetic activity, covering their structural diversity and the multiple diabetes-relevant targets they modulate, such as those involved in hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and β-cell dysfunction. It critically assesses the available evidence for these compounds as potential type 2 diabetes therapeutics, though the work is descriptive and preclinical in scope.

papers.title: Conformational Sampling of CPT1A Enables Dynamic Structure-Based Ligand Screening.
papers.abstract: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) catalyzes a rate-limiting step in fatty acid β-oxidation and is a target for studies of metabolic disease and cancer. However, the structural dynamics of CPT1A remain poorly understood due to the lack of full-length structure. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Markov state models (MSMs), and binding free energy calculations to elucidate the conformational landscape of human CPT1A. We performed an all-atom MD simulation of CPT1A embedded in a realistic outer mitochondrial membr
papers.summary: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations, Markov state models, and binding free energy calculations to map the conformational landscape of full-length human CPT1A embedded in a mitochondrial membrane. The authors identify distinct conformational states that could guide structure-based ligand screening for this metabolic and cancer target. The work provides a dynamic structural framework for CPT1A where no full-length experimental structure exists.

papers.title: Rational Design and Delivery of Engineered Peptides: Toward a Unified Framework for Structure, Screening, and Application.
papers.abstract: This review presents a three-tiered engineering framework that systematically addresses these barriers. First, we survey chemical and sequence-based stabilization strategies, including lipidation, backbone N-methylation, and cyclization, that convert labile natural peptides into protease-resistant scaffolds. Second, moving beyond generic stabilization, we dissect the rational design of effector-inhibitory peptides, with particular emphasis on disulfide bond topology engineering as a powerful means to lock binding-competent conformations, alongside structure-guided interface optimization. Third
papers.summary: This review proposes a three-tiered framework for engineering therapeutic peptides: chemical and sequence-based stabilization strategies (lipidation, backbone N-methylation, cyclization) to improve protease resistance, rational design of effector-inhibitory peptides with emphasis on disulfide bond topology engineering to lock binding-competent conformations, and structure-guided interface optimization. It aims to unify structure, screening, and application considerations for peptide drug design.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of Novel Peptides Targeting Protein Disulfide Isomerase as Antiplatelet Agents.
papers.abstract: Extracellular protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) is a critical mediator of thrombus formation and a promising target for novel antithrombotic therapies aiming to overcome the bleeding risks associated with current antiplatelet agents. This study aimed to design and evaluate novel, targeted peptide-based PDI inhibitors with a safe physiological profile. We utilized a bioinformatics-driven rational design approach, based on the evolutionary conservation of the PDI active site, to generate a library of 34 targeted peptides. The inhibitory mechanism and biological efficacy of the lead candidate, pe
papers.summary: The authors used evolutionary conservation of the PDI active site to rationally design 34 peptides, then characterized a lead candidate as an inhibitor of extracellular PDI. The goal is a safer antiplatelet/antithrombotic agent that avoids the bleeding risks of current antiplatelet drugs. The work is a design-and-evaluation study of peptide PDI inhibitors with in vitro biological characterization.

papers.title: Screening and identification of a novel umami peptide with in vitro anti-inflammatory potential from sea cucumber protein: Integration of flavoromics, bioinformatic prediction, molecular simulation and experimental validation.
papers.abstract: Sea cucumber protein was sequentially hydrolyzed with pepsin, trypsin, and enterokinase to obtain peptides with desirable taste characteristics and immunomodulatory potential. Multi-scale characterization, flavoromics, peptidomics, bioinformatic screening, molecular simulations, and cellular assays were employed to investigate the structural changes, flavor remodeling, and bioactivity of the resulting hydrolysates. Results showed that hydrolysis disrupted the compact protein structure, induced conformational unfolding, and yielded short peptides (0.5-1.5 kDa) with enhanced hydrophilicity and p
papers.summary: This study used a multi-step enzymatic hydrolysis of sea cucumber protein to generate short peptides (0.5–1.5 kDa) with improved taste and immunomodulatory properties. By combining flavoromics, peptidomics, bioinformatic screening, molecular simulations, and cell assays, the authors identified a novel umami peptide with in vitro anti-inflammatory activity. The work demonstrates an integrated pipeline for discovering bioactive food-derived peptides with dual flavor and health benefits.

papers.title: Graph-theoretic microstate analysis reveals altered dynamics in common-cation mixed electrolytes.
papers.abstract: Mixed aqueous electrolytes are increasingly valuable in industrial applications, where they often behave very differently from their single-salt counterparts, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we present a comprehensive molecular dynamics simulation study of ion networks in NaNO2(aq), NaNO3(aq), and their mixtures. New graph-theoretic workflows combined with principal component analysis identify ion aggregate macro-states, based on number of cations in the cluster, and microstates, based on inter-ion connectivity patterns, enabling detailed investigation of state tr
papers.summary: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations and new graph-theoretic workflows combined with principal component analysis to characterize ion aggregation in mixed aqueous electrolytes (NaNO2, NaNO3, and their mixtures). The authors identify macro-states (based on cation cluster size) and microstates (based on inter-ion connectivity patterns), revealing altered dynamics in mixed versus single-salt electrolytes. The work offers a methodological framework for understanding why mixed electrolytes behave differently from their single-salt counterparts.

papers.title: Imidazo[1,2-b]Pyrazole-1,2,4-oxadiazole Linked 1,2,3-Triazoles: Synthesis, Antibacterial, Biofilm, and In Silico Studies.
papers.abstract: The growing incidence of bacterial resistance, especially in gram-positive infections, emphasizes how urgently new antibacterial medicines must be developed. This study presents the rational design and synthesis of a series of fused imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazole-1,2,4-oxadiazole-1,2,3-triazole hybrids (8a-8n) employing a multi-step synthetic approach that includes oxidative cyclisation, amidoxime formation, Vilsmeier-mediated cyclodehydration, and Cu(I)-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC). The synthesized compounds were assessed for their in vitro antibacterial efficacy against Bacillus subt
papers.summary: This study reports the design and synthesis of a series of fused imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazole-1,2,4-oxadiazole-1,2,3-triazole hybrid compounds using a multi-step approach including CuAAC click chemistry. The compounds were evaluated for in vitro antibacterial activity against Bacillus subtilis and other strains, with additional biofilm and in silico docking studies. The work aims to address the growing problem of gram-positive bacterial resistance by identifying new antibacterial scaffolds.

papers.title: Green Extraction of Phenolic Compounds From Pistacia lentiscus Leaves Coupled With LC-MS Characterization and Structure-Based Enzyme Inhibition Analysis.
papers.abstract: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and urease are critical enzymes involved in various pathological conditions associated with cellular and tissue damage. Natural products are increasingly explored as safer alternatives to synthetic inhibitors. This study evaluates the phytochemical composition and enzyme inhibitory potential of Pistacia lentiscus leaves using a green extraction approach. Bioactive compounds were extracted via lactic acid-assisted ultrasound, and the crude extract was characterized for total phenolics, flavonoids, LC-MS profile, and in vitro inhibition of acetylcholinesterase and ure
papers.summary: This study used a green lactic acid-assisted ultrasound extraction to obtain phenolic compounds from Pistacia lentiscus leaves, then characterized the extract by LC-MS and tested its ability to inhibit acetylcholinesterase and urease. The work links phytochemical profiling with in vitro enzyme inhibition and structure-based analysis, supporting the leaves as a source of natural enzyme inhibitors.

papers.title: Network pharmacology-driven identification of PTP1β and rational design of simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors for neuroprotection in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that predominantly affects elderly people and is characterized by cognitive decline and dementia. Protein tyrosine phosphatase-1B (PTP1B) is known to modulate pro-inflammatory mediators, and its overexpression in the brain has been implicated in AD-associated neuroinflammation. This study explores the mechanism of A20, A26, and co-crystal-designed compound targeting non-competitive allosteric PTP1B enzyme inhibition for AD therapy using network pharmacology and computational studies. Protein-protein interaction was designed f
papers.summary: This study uses network pharmacology and computational docking to identify PTP1B as a target for Alzheimer's disease neuroinflammation and to design simufilam-based allosteric inhibitors. The authors propose that non-competitive allosteric inhibition of PTP1B by these compounds could provide neuroprotection, though the work is entirely computational with no experimental validation.

papers.title: Structural insights into an aptainhibitor of the SARS-CoV-2 E protein using molecular docking, molecular dynamics, and biophysical analyses.
papers.abstract: The envelope (E) protein is a highly conserved structural protein that plays key roles in viral assembly, membrane curvature, and pathogenesis. The E-protein transmembrane (TM) domain oligomerizes into a pentameric ion channel, which contributes to the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome that is directly linked to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Therefore, targeted disruption of E-protein oligomerization represents a powerful therapeutic strategy to attenuate viral virulence. In this study, we report the first DNA aptainhibitors to block E-protein oligomerization. The lead aptainh
papers.summary: This study reports the first DNA aptamers designed to block oligomerization of the SARS-CoV-2 envelope (E) protein, whose pentameric ion channel activity contributes to inflammasome activation and ARDS. Using molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and biophysical analyses, the authors characterize how the lead aptamer binds and disrupts E-protein assembly. The work suggests a potential therapeutic strategy for attenuating SARS-CoV-2 virulence by targeting a conserved structural protein.

papers.title: Clodronate and trehalose exhibit a paradoxical antagonistic interaction that suppresses proliferation of canine mammary tumour cells.
papers.abstract: Clodronate and trehalose are known to modulate metabolic and autophagy-related pathways, respectively, yet their combined effects on tumour cell proliferation remain poorly understood. This study investigated the individual and combined effects of these compounds on the canine mammary tumour cell line CMT-U27 and explored underlying mechanisms using network pharmacology. Cell proliferation was assessed following treatment with clodronate, trehalose, and their combination across a range of concentrations. Growth rate analysis and Bliss independence modelling were used to evaluate drug interacti
papers.summary: This study tested clodronate and trehalose, alone and in combination, on the canine mammary tumour cell line CMT-U27. Unexpectedly, the two compounds interacted antagonistically, suppressing tumour cell proliferation more than either alone would predict under a simple additive model, and network pharmacology was used to probe the underlying mechanisms. The finding suggests a paradoxical drug interaction that may be relevant to repurposing these compounds in veterinary oncology.

papers.title: A single amino acid mutation alters substrate specificity towards l-glucose in a bacterial l-galactose dehydrogenase.
papers.abstract: Structure-based mutagenesis was performed to modify the substrate specificity of bacterial l-galactose dehydrogenase from Luteolibacter sp. strain LG18, which also exhibits intrinsic l-glucose dehydrogenase activity. Based on previously reported crystal structures of the enzyme in ternary complex with l-galactose or l-glucose and NADP+, an M212Q mutant was generated and found to exhibit a pronounced preference for l-glucose. Kinetic analysis showed that the M212Q mutant displayed an approximately 20-fold higher k cat/K M value for l-glucose than for l-galactose. To elucidate the structural bas
papers.summary: Researchers used structure-based mutagenesis to alter the substrate specificity of a bacterial L-galactose dehydrogenase that also has intrinsic L-glucose dehydrogenase activity. The single M212Q mutation shifted the enzyme's preference toward L-glucose, yielding an approximately 20-fold higher catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for L-glucose over L-galactose. This demonstrates that a single amino acid change can substantially redirect substrate specificity in this enzyme family.

papers.title: Rational structure-guided identification of a Bcl-2-targeting peptide with antiproliferative effects on colorectal cancer cells.
papers.abstract: Bcl-2 is critical for tumour survival and serves as a promising anticancer drug target. Herein, a series of novel Bcl-2-targeted peptides were identified through structure-based virtual screening and systematic biological validation. Four candidate peptides were selected from the peptide library. MST results demonstrated that Peptide 1 exhibited the strongest apparent binding affinity towards Bcl-2 (Kd = 0.51 ± 0.03 μM), superior to VS-9 and other screened peptides. Molecular dynamics simulation, free energy landscape analysis, and MM/GBSA calculation further supported the predicted conformati
papers.journal: Journal of enzyme inhibition and medicinal chemistry
papers.summary: The authors used structure-based virtual screening to identify peptides that bind Bcl-2, a key anti-apoptotic protein in cancer, then validated the top candidates experimentally. Peptide 1 showed the strongest binding affinity (Kd ≈ 0.51 µM), better than the reference compound VS-9, and molecular dynamics simulations supported the predicted binding mode. The peptide also inhibited proliferation of colorectal cancer cells, suggesting a starting point for Bcl-2-targeting anticancer peptide development.

papers.title: MEMO1-ERα interaction may occur independent of Y537 phosphorylation which differs from MEMO1-ErbB2 binding.
papers.abstract: MEMO1 is a protein implicated in cancer-associated signaling through interactions with other proteins, including estrogen receptor α (ERα). We used fluorescence polarization, molecular dynamics simulations, and protein pull-down assays to characterize the interaction between MEMO1 and ERα. MEMO1 bound to an ERα peptide containing phosphorylated Y537 but unexpectedly showed comparable affinity for the non-phosphorylated peptide. Computational modeling identified distinct binding modes and suggested contributions from MEMO1 residues. Pull-down experiments confirmed interaction between MEMO1 and
papers.summary: This study characterizes how the protein MEMO1 binds to estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), a key cancer signaling protein. Using fluorescence polarization, molecular dynamics, and pull-down assays, the authors find that MEMO1 binds an ERα peptide containing phosphorylated Y537, but surprisingly with similar affinity to the non-phosphorylated version—suggesting the interaction does not depend on Y537 phosphorylation, unlike MEMO1's binding to ErbB2. Computational modeling revealed distinct binding modes and implicated specific MEMO1 residues.

papers.title: Targeting Muscle-Specific E3 Ligases in Cancer Cachexia Through Structure-Based Virtual Screening of Small-Molecule Inhibitors.
papers.abstract: Cachexia is a multifactorial metabolic syndrome characterized by severe skeletal muscle loss that cannot be reversed by nutritional support. Common in cancer and other chronic diseases, it significantly increases morbidity and mortality. Muscle wasting is primarily driven by activation of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway through the E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which promote protein degradation and muscle atrophy. This study used computational modeling and docking to identify small-molecule inhibitors targeting these ligases, including repurposed drugs with anti-cachectic potentia
papers.summary: This study used computational docking and virtual screening to identify small-molecule inhibitors targeting the muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases MuRF1 and Atrogin-1, which drive protein degradation in cancer cachexia. The authors propose candidate compounds, including repurposed drugs, as potential anti-cachectic agents. The work is purely computational and lacks experimental validation.

papers.title: Potential Molecular Links Between Benzophenone-3 and Breast Cancer: Network Toxicology, Machine Learning, Molecular Modeling, and Gene Expression Validation.
papers.abstract: Benzophenone-3 (BP-3) is a widely used ultraviolet filter with potential carcinogenic concern, but its molecular link with breast cancer remains unclear. This study aimed to identify candidate targets and potential molecular links between BP-3 and breast cancer using toxicological prediction, machine learning, molecular modeling, and gene expression analysis.
papers.summary: This study integrates network toxicology, machine learning, molecular docking/modeling, and gene expression analysis to identify candidate molecular targets linking the UV filter benzophenone-3 (BP-3) to breast cancer. It proposes potential target genes and pathways through which BP-3 exposure might contribute to breast carcinogenesis, though the findings are computational predictions with limited experimental validation.

papers.title: Mechanism of luteolin in treating chronic heart failure by regulating HIF-1 signaling pathway-mediated mitochondrial damage to inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis.
papers.abstract: Chronic heart failure (CHF) is a systemic cardiovascular disease characterized by an extremely poor prognosis. Luteolin demonstrates promising therapeutic potential in the prevention and management of CHF. This study aims to explore the mechanism by which luteolin ameliorates CHF through mitigating mitochondrial damage and inhibiting cardiomyocyte apoptosis, using bioinformatics analysis combined with in vitro and in vivo experiments.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
papers.summary: This study investigates how luteolin, a plant flavonoid, protects against chronic heart failure by targeting the HIF-1 signaling pathway. Using bioinformatics plus cell and animal experiments, the authors show that luteolin reduces mitochondrial damage and cardiomyocyte apoptosis, suggesting HIF-1 pathway modulation as the underlying mechanism. The work supports luteolin as a potential therapeutic candidate for CHF.

papers.title: Artificially intelligent modeling of macromolecular assemblies.
papers.abstract: The study of macromolecular assembly formation is one of the most challenging tasks in computational modeling as it requires extensive exploration of conformational and configurational space, especially when driven by conformational transitions or folding instabilities, which are typically associated with high energy barriers. Although this type of study has traditionally been addressed in silico by using techniques that reduce the computational cost of simulations, such as coarse-grained models, artificial intelligence (AI) has recently entered the field at multiple levels, aiding in paramete
papers.summary: This review examines how artificial intelligence is being integrated into computational modeling of macromolecular assembly formation, a problem that requires exploring vast conformational and configurational spaces often hindered by high energy barriers. It discusses AI applications at multiple levels, including parameterization and simulation acceleration, as alternatives or complements to traditional coarse-grained approaches. The paper provides an overview of emerging AI-driven strategies for tackling complex assembly dynamics.

papers.title: Correction: Metals-triggered compound CDPDP exhibits anti-arthritic behavior by downregulating the inflammatory cytokines, and modulating the oxidative storm in mice models with extensive ADMET, docking and simulation studies.
papers.abstract: [This corrects the article DOI: 10.3389/fphar.2022.1053744.].
papers.summary: This is a correction notice for a previously published article on the compound CDPDP, which was reported to have anti-arthritic effects in mice through downregulation of inflammatory cytokines and modulation of oxidative stress, supported by ADMET, docking, and simulation studies. The correction likely addresses errors or omissions in the original publication; the abstract provides no new scientific findings.

papers.title: Exploring the potential targets and possible mechanisms of Shenqi Fuzheng Injection in the treatment of cancer-associated muscle wasting based on network pharmacology.
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated muscle wasting (CAMW) is a debilitating condition observed in cancer patients, characterized by progressive skeletal muscle loss driven by tumor-secreted inflammatory cytokines, metabolic reprogramming, and enhanced apoptotic signaling, severely affecting the quality of life of patients. Shenqi Fuzheng Injection (SFI) is a traditional Chinese medicine preparation made from Codonopsis pilosula (Dangshen) and Astragalus membranaceus (Huangqi) in specific proportions, which has the effects of replenishing qi, strengthening the body, alleviating the side effects of radiotherapy a
papers.summary: This study used network pharmacology to predict which molecular targets and pathways might mediate the effects of Shenqi Fuzheng Injection (a traditional Chinese medicine made from Codonopsis pilosula and Astragalus membranaceus) on cancer-associated muscle wasting. The approach identifies candidate targets and mechanisms computationally rather than through direct experimental validation, suggesting potential pathways for future testing. The work is exploratory and hypothesis-generating, with limited experimental confirmation.

papers.title: Mechanistic study on components of Angelica Pubescens-Taxillus Chinensis in improving compression-induced intervertebral disc degeneration via piezo1/NF-κB signaling axis.
papers.abstract: Abnormal mechanical load is a critical risk factor for intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD), and nucleus pulposus (NP) cell senescence is a core pathogenic mechanism in IVDD. Piezo1 is a mechanosensitive ion channel, whereas the NF-κB pathway promotes cellular senescence. The classical formula Duhuo Jisheng decoction has shown potential benefits in IVDD-related conditions, and its core herbal pair Angelica Pubescens-Taxillus Chinensis accounting for its pivotal therapeutic effects.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
papers.summary: This study investigates how the herbal pair Angelica Pubescens-Taxillus Chinensis (from the Duhuo Jisheng decoction) protects against compression-induced intervertebral disc degeneration. The authors propose that the herbal components act through the Piezo1 mechanosensitive ion channel and the NF-κB senescence pathway, linking mechanical stress sensing to disc cell aging.

papers.title: Peptide optimization to improve antigen presentation and antitumor responses in sarcoma.
papers.abstract: Sarcomas are rare and heterogeneous malignancies for which therapeutic options remain limited, particularly in advanced disease. Standard treatments, including surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and approved targeted agents, provide marginal improvements in progression-free and overall survival, highlighting the need for immunotherapeutic strategies. Therapeutic cancer vaccines represent a promising strategy, but clinical efficacy has been limited by low antigen immunogenicity and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Enhancing antigen presentation and T-cell receptor (TCR) enga
papers.summary: This paper describes peptide optimization strategies aimed at improving antigen presentation and T-cell receptor engagement for sarcoma cancer vaccines. The work addresses the limited immunogenicity of sarcoma antigens and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which have hampered vaccine efficacy. By engineering peptides to enhance presentation and antitumor responses, the study offers a potential route to more effective immunotherapies for these rare cancers.

papers.title: Integrated toxicogenomic and single-nucleus transcriptomic analyses prioritize SDHB and NDUFAB1 in mitochondrial respiration-associated remodeling during cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury.
papers.abstract: Cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury (Cis-AKI) is a multifactorial nephrotoxic syndrome involving proximal tubular injury, oxidative and inflammatory stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, metabolic disturbance, and regulated cell death. However, the molecular targets linking cisplatin-associated toxicogenomic changes to AKI remain incompletely characterized.
papers.journal: Frontiers in cell and developmental biology
papers.summary: This study integrates toxicogenomic data with single-nucleus transcriptomics to identify molecular drivers of mitochondrial dysfunction in cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury. The authors prioritize SDHB and NDUFAB1 as key genes involved in mitochondrial respiration-associated remodeling, highlighting them as potential targets linking cisplatin toxicity to tubular injury.

papers.title: Discovery of metabolite biomarkers for cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury based on metabolomics: neurotoxic mechanism and functional validation of a flavopiridol -related metabolite.
papers.abstract: To investigate the role and potential mechanism of metabolite alterations during cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) and to explore novel candidate molecular markers for the diagnosis of this disease.
papers.summary: This study uses metabolomics to identify metabolite changes in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury and discovers a flavopiridol-related metabolite as a potential diagnostic biomarker. The authors further validate its functional role and propose a neurotoxic mechanism, suggesting new avenues for biomarker development and therapeutic targeting in stroke.

papers.title: Mapping the major B-cell linear epitope of silkworm (Bombyx mori) pupal chitinase and molecular dynamics insights into its IgE-binding stability.
papers.abstract: As domestic silkworm (Bombyx mori) pupae emerge as a promising alternative food source, the severe IgE-mediated allergic reactions they trigger have raised significant public health concerns. Despite the identification of the novel allergen Bombyx mori chitinase (BmChi), its precise linear B-cell epitopes and molecular mechanisms of IgE recognition remain uncharacterized. In this hypothesis-generating study, we systematically mapped the linear B-cell epitopes of BmChi and evaluated their structural dynamics. Following bioinformatic predictions, a high-resolution in vitro screening using 109 ov
papers.summary: This study maps the linear B-cell epitopes of Bombyx mori pupal chitinase (BmChi), a newly identified allergen in silkworm pupae that are being explored as an alternative food source. Using bioinformatic prediction followed by in vitro screening with sera from allergic individuals, the authors identify a major IgE-binding epitope and use molecular dynamics simulations to assess the structural stability of its IgE interaction. The work provides the first epitope-level characterization of BmChi and offers a basis for allergen risk assessment and potential epitope-based diagnostics or therapeutics.

papers.title: Structure-based discovery of a novel Granzyme A (GZMA) inhibitor for autism spectrum disorder through integrative transcriptomics, virtual screening, and long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.abstract: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a trypsin-like serine protease expressed in cytotoxic lymphocytes that cleaves gasdermin B (GSDMB) to release a pore-forming N-terminal fragment, thereby inducing pyroptosis, a lytic and pro-inflammatory form of programmed cell death. This pathway has been implicated in immune dysregulation reported in a subset of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). In this study, we reanalyzed the peripheral blood transcriptome dataset GSE26415 using an integrative computational framework comprising outlier-aware quality control, differential expression analysis, functional e
papers.summary: The authors reanalyzed a peripheral blood transcriptome dataset from autism spectrum disorder (ASD) patients and identified Granzyme A (GZMA), a serine protease that triggers pyroptosis via gasdermin B cleavage, as a potential drug target linked to immune dysregulation. They then used structure-based virtual screening and long-timescale molecular dynamics simulations to discover a novel small-molecule GZMA inhibitor. The work is entirely computational, with no experimental validation of the compound's activity or efficacy.
